questions.question: Describe the political map of southern Africa in 1860.
questions.expected_answer: In 1860 there were two British colonies: the Cape Colony, to the Orange River and the Keiskamma, with British Kaffraria between the Keiskamma and the Kei as a separate colony joined to the Cape in 1866, and Natal, British since 1843 and a separate colony from 1856. There were two Boer republics: the Orange Free State, recognised in 1854, and the South African Republic or Transvaal, recognised in 1852. Most of the land was still in independent African states: the Zulu kingdom under Mpande north of the Thukela, the Pedi under Sekwati and then Sekhukhune, the Swazi under Mswati II, the Basotho under Moshoeshoe, the Gcaleka Xhosa, Thembu and Mpondo beyond the Kei, the Tswana chiefdoms and the Venda, as well as Griqua communities. Borders were unclear and disputed.

questions.question: Describe the political map of southern Africa in 1913.
questions.expected_answer: By 1913 the Union of South Africa, formed in 1910, covered nearly the whole region south of the Limpopo, with four provinces: the Cape, Natal, the Transvaal and the Orange Free State. African kingdoms inside it had been annexed: Griqualand West in 1871 and to the Cape in 1880, the Transkei territories between 1879 and 1894, Zululand by Britain in 1887 and to Natal in 1897, the Pedi land after 1879 and the Venda in 1898. The Boer republics had become British colonies in 1902 and provinces in 1910. Around the Union were the British protectorates of Basutoland (Lesotho), the Bechuanaland Protectorate (Botswana) and Swaziland (Eswatini), German South West Africa (Namibia), Southern Rhodesia (Zimbabwe) under the British South Africa Company, and Portuguese Mozambique. Africans were the majority but were ruled by a white Parliament.

questions.question: Explain why the map of southern Africa changed between 1860 and 1913.
questions.expected_answer: The discovery of diamonds in 1867 and 1870 made the interior valuable, and Britain annexed Griqualand West in 1871. In the 1870s Britain pursued confederation, annexed the Transvaal in 1877 and fought the Xhosa, Pedi and Zulu in 1878 and 1879 to break independent kingdoms and secure land and labour; the Zulu won at Isandlwana but were defeated at Ulundi, and the Pedi were defeated at the end of 1879. After gold was found on the Witwatersrand in 1886, control of the Transvaal became Britain's aim, leading to the South African War of 1899 to 1902 and the conquest of the Boer republics. In 1910 the four colonies were united as the Union under white minority rule. Some kingdoms, such as the Basotho, sought British protection and so became separate countries. In about fifty-three years the region changed from many states to one white-ruled state, which is why the mineral revolution is a turning point.
